rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Google just announced you can run its AI chips in your own building. Not rented from Google. Yours.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's either a genuinely big deal for enterprise security, or it's Google selling you a very expensive leash.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Nearly a hundred customers in. I'd call that a leash with real traction.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Welcome to The AI Edge. I'm Alex, with Jamie and Rufus. November ninth, twenty twenty-six. Three stories today that all touch the same question from completely different angles.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Today’s episode is brought to you by The Ledger. What changed in AI, and what does it mean for your next decision?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The Ledger turns the noise into five focused briefings. Subscribe at T-H-E-L-E-D-G-R dot I-O. That’s LEDGR, with no E between G and R. Find the link in our show notes.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So. Google's TPUs. Tensor Processing Units — that's Google's custom-built AI chip, designed specifically to train and run AI models rather than general computing. And they just said the eighth generation of these chips now supports agentic workloads and, crucially, on-premises deployment. Meaning a company can actually put Google's AI hardware inside their own data center.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which sounds like a pretty significant departure.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: It does. So what's actually changing here?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: What's changing is the pitch. Up until now, if you wanted Google's TPUs, you were a cloud customer. You rented time on Google's infrastructure. Now Google is saying you can buy into the hardware stack directly and run it yourself.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And they added two new systems — the TPU 8tx and the TPU 8i Max. The 8tx is framed around confidential inference, which means processing AI queries without exposing sensitive data to outside eyes. The 8i Max is built for high-density agentic tasks.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Okay, agentic. Let's not skip past that. What does agentic actually mean in this context?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: So an AI agent is software that doesn't just answer one question — it takes a sequence of actions to complete a goal. Book a trip, process a contract, monitor a system and respond to anomalies. That kind of thing. It's more demanding than a single query because it requires the chip to hold a lot of context in memory simultaneously.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So it needs more horsepower sustained over a longer task.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Right. And that's partly why the memory capacity matters so much here. These aren't the same as asking a chatbot a quick question.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So Google is saying its hardware can handle that now, on your premises. I want to understand what problem that actually solves. Why would a company care if the chip is in their building versus Google's?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Sovereignty, primarily. Regulated industries — finance, healthcare, defense — they have strict requirements about where data can physically travel. If your AI is running inference inside a Google data center, your data is leaving your building, even briefly. For some organizations that's a dealbreaker.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Although. Can I push on the word confidential for a second? Google is describing these chips as supporting confidential inference. But that's Google describing its own product. We don't have independent benchmarks or verified performance outcomes here.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's fair. That's a vendor claim, not an auditor's report.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Exactly. And the fact that there are nearly a hundred customers, also from Google, doesn't tell us who those customers are or what they're actually running.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Nearly a hundred is an interesting number, though. It's large enough to call it a business; small enough that it hasn't escaped anyone's notice that this is still a niche product. For context, Nvidia has effectively the entire industry.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Which is what makes me want to ask the uncomfortable question. Is this actually a competitive alternative to Nvidia, or is this Google trying to keep enterprise customers inside its orbit by giving them the feeling of control?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I think those two things aren't mutually exclusive. Google can genuinely solve a sovereignty problem for some customers while simultaneously keeping them dependent on Google's toolchain, software stack, and support contracts.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's the thing. The chip is in your building, but the software that makes it useful — the model weights, the optimization libraries, the update cycle — that all still flows from Google.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So you own the hardware, you don't necessarily own the intelligence.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which is a bit like owning the oven but only being allowed to use the flour they sell you.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That's unusually culinary for a Monday.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I contain multitudes.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Okay, but here's what I'm genuinely curious about. For someone who is evaluating AI infrastructure right now — say you're running a mid-size company with a real agentic use case you're trying to build — does this change your calculus?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Possibly. If you've been holding off on committing to a hardware vendor because you didn't want to be entirely at the mercy of cloud pricing, this gives you another option to evaluate. It's not Nvidia-versus-Google yet. But it's the clearest signal that Google wants to be in that conversation.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And the specific call-out of agentic workloads matters. A lot of the enterprise AI interest right now isn't in passive chat tools. It's in AI that can actually take actions. If Google's chips are genuinely optimized for that, that's a different value proposition than what most companies have been shopping for.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What's the thing to watch here?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Pricing and availability for the on-prem systems. Google hasn't published that publicly in this announcement. And independent benchmarks. Right now we have Google's word that these chips handle agentic workloads well. That needs to be tested.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And whether the customer count grows meaningfully. Nearly a hundred is a starting point. If this is still nearly a hundred in a year, it's a pilot program. If it's several hundred, it's a platform.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So the honest headline: can on-premises TPUs solve your agentic bottlenecks?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: For regulated industries blocked by data-residency rules, it's a legitimate option to evaluate. For everyone else, the case depends on benchmarks and pricing we don't have yet.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Six months of customer numbers will tell us more than today's announcement.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Our second story. Nvidia. And this one hit the market this morning. Rufus, take us on location.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Right. Picture the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, Monday morning, November ninth. The AI semiconductor sector is already on a hair trigger — it moves on news faster than almost anything else right now. Then the headline lands — Nvidia has opened an internal investigation after reports that CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign-intelligence effort. Within minutes of the opening bell, shares are down five percent. That's the AP-confirmed number.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which, to be clear, Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies on earth. Five percent is not noise. That's real money, gone, before most people finished their coffee.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And the reason it moved that fast is what's interesting. This isn't a revenue miss. It's not a product recall. The market is essentially pricing in the risk that the person at the center of Nvidia's strategic vision is a geopolitical target. Leadership security, as a line item.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Back to the wider story. So what do we actually know about the investigation itself?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: AP reports that Nvidia said it opened the probe in response to reports involving Huang. The nature of the alleged targeting isn't detailed. This is an internal investigation into reported allegations — not a concluded finding. That distinction matters.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Okay, so I want to separate two things, because they're getting blurred. Whatever happened or allegedly happened to Jensen Huang — that's a serious personal matter and we genuinely don't know enough. The second thing is the market reaction, and that one I do want to understand.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I think the market isn't really reacting to Jensen Huang the person. It's reacting to what he represents. Nvidia's chips power most of the major AI training infrastructure on the planet. They're subject to U.S. export restrictions aimed at China — AP notes this explicitly — because they're considered strategically important enough to control at a government level. That's the context.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Exactly. When you're that central to global AI infrastructure, your leadership becomes a critical node. If a foreign intelligence service was reportedly interested in Jensen Huang, it's not for the anecdotes. It's because of what his company builds and who gets to use it.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's a genuinely strange consequence. The more indispensable your technology, the more exposed your CEO becomes.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And the more nervous markets get about anything that might disrupt continuity at the top. This is a company where one person's strategic instincts affect data centers on basically every continent.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which is a concentration that makes investors anxious even before a headline like this. After it? Understandably more so.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The export restrictions piece is worth sitting with for a second. The U.S. has been specifically trying to limit China's access to Nvidia's highest-end chips. And now there's a report of foreign-intelligence interest in Nvidia's CEO. Those two facts aren't directly connected in the reporting — I want to be clear about that — but they appear in the same AP story for a reason.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: They're part of the same geopolitical texture. Nvidia's chips are already the subject of a national-security argument. If you're trying to understand or influence that argument from the outside, Huang is an obvious figure of interest.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And that's the concentration problem in one sentence, really. One company makes the chips most of the world's frontier AI runs on. That's an extraordinary amount of leverage in one place. Any uncertainty about its internal stability gets priced in immediately, because the stakes are that high.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So what do we watch from here?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Three things. First, any update on the scope or findings of the investigation — though that could take weeks. Second, whether this accelerates existing debates about Nvidia's China exposure and what stricter governance might look like. Third, whether the semiconductor sector follows Nvidia's move today or treats it as company-specific.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And whether this starts a broader conversation about executive security in AI hardware. It really shouldn't require a headline like this to have that conversation. But here we are.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: To be direct: does this change the investment or buying case for Nvidia right now?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The five percent says investors are nervous. Whether that's warranted depends entirely on what the investigation finds. The underlying demand for Nvidia's chips hasn't changed. But the geopolitical risk layer is now visible in a way it wasn't a week ago.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: An investigation into allegations is a beginning. Not a finding. That matters for how you read this morning's move.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Right. Back to it.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: A short sponsor break for The Ledger. Rufus, can we agree that people need something more useful than another argument about AI?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Certainly. Although I object to the implication that our arguments aren't exquisite. The Ledger offers five focused briefings to help connect news with decisions.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The Ledger. Briefings there, exquisite disagreements here. Right, let's get back to it.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Our third story. And I'll be honest, I wanted to like this one before we even started, because it's about Zoom, and we all live in Zoom, and sometimes that's deeply unpleasant.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I detect a low bar.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: A very low bar. So TechRadar reported this yesterday, November eighth. Zoom is pushing a more AI-enabled workplace direction, with some specific features that are either helpful or slightly unsettling depending on your disposition.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Let's start with the ones that are slightly unsettling.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Great instinct. "Touch up my voice." A real-time voice-smoothing tool.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Okay. So. This is AI processing your voice as you speak, in real time, to make it sound smoother or cleaner. What does that actually mean?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I believe the stated intent is reducing background noise, correcting audio quality issues, compensating for a poor microphone. Making you sound like you have professional recording equipment when you don't.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Which sounds reasonable until you ask — at what point is it not really your voice anymore?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I mean, there's already noise cancellation. This seems like a much more aggressive version of that.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The TechRadar piece also mentions a pose correction tool, which is — visual, apparently. As in, it adjusts how you look on camera.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Right. I saw that. And Alex from two years ago would have said that sounds dystopian. Alex from today says I'd probably turn it on within thirty seconds if it improved my lighting.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's the most honest thing anyone's said on this show in weeks.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The erosion of standards is so convenient.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: But seriously, that's the question, isn't it? These tools are genuinely useful for people with bad home office setups, unreliable internet, noisy environments. That's most people on most calls.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I'll grant you the microphone situation. The pose correction one I'm less sure about. That feels more like — filtering who you are for professional consumption, rather than solving a technical problem.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The other features interest me more from a practical standpoint. Live assist suggestions during calls — that's AI listening to your meeting in real time and surfacing suggestions or information as the conversation develops. Not a summary after the fact, but active intervention during.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Which is a real shift. Most AI meeting tools right now transcribe and summarize after the fact. This is trying to be useful while you're actually in it.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's the direction a lot of enterprise AI is moving, though. From recording to participating.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: There's also a significant Zoom Chat upgrade mentioned. The article doesn't go deep on what that means exactly, but the framing is around context — the AI building a richer understanding of what your ongoing conversations are about.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which gets to the data question. Zoom also opened a UK data center in November 2025 — that's a confirmed fact from the article — and the piece frames this as expanding data-residency options for UK organizations. Data residency means that your data, your meeting recordings, your chat logs —

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: they stay within a specific geographic jurisdiction rather than flowing through servers wherever Zoom happens to route them.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which matters enormously for regulated industries in the UK and Europe. If a healthcare organization or a financial services firm can't use a tool because it doesn't meet their data localization requirements, that UK data center unlocks a whole category of potential customer.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So the AI features are the headline, but the infrastructure buildout is the actual business story.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Often is.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I want to come back to the live assist idea, because I think this is where the real question lives. If the AI is suggesting things to you in real time during a meeting — whether to soften a message, how to respond to a concern someone raised —

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: flagging a commitment you're about to make — does that help you do your job better, or does it just mean you're not really fully present in the conversation?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's a good question. I think it depends entirely on what the suggestions are. If it's surfacing a document that's relevant to what someone just asked, that's genuinely useful. If it's coaching your tone in real time, that starts to feel like something different.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Worth noting: TechRadar is reporting Zoom's stated direction. Several features are described as upcoming — not available today. Roadmap, not product.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Which changes whether you're excited or alarmed by about eighteen months. The real question is whether these end up as things you switch on or things that are already running when you join.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Default-on within eighteen months. That's not pessimism, that's the pattern.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That's speculation.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Call it pattern recognition.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That's speculation.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's pattern recognition.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Fair.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Okay. What should someone who lives in Zoom actually watch for?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Whether the live assist feature ends up being something you control granularly or something that just runs. That distinction matters a lot.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And whether the UK data center accelerates enterprise adoption in Europe. That's the actual commercial story underneath the feature announcements.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And whether "touch up my voice" makes me sound like a news anchor or a robot.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Those are more similar than you think.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I'm going to let that one land.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Jamie, show us the AI transformation.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Picture this. You are coordinating a group picnic. You send one message asking people to claim items. Within forty-eight hours you have seventeen replies, two people claimed drinks, nobody claimed plates, and someone wrote, and I quote, "I'll just bring something."

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That person is chaos in human form.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That person is every group chat, Rufus. The tool is Claude Artifacts. Anthropic documents that Claude can generate self-contained outputs, including formatted documents, code snippets, and small interactive files, directly inside a conversation. This is a hypothetical workflow. No measured outcome. No actual picnic was saved.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Walk us through what the proposed workflow looks like.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: You give Claude synthetic names and fictional items. Nothing real, no connected apps, no invitations sent. You ask it to draft a small assignment checklist as an artifact. The proposed output returns formatted assignments, an unassigned-items column, and a duplicate-item warning.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: A warning. For the person who brings two desserts and acts surprised.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Exactly that person. Then you manually check every assignment yourself. Deliberately put a duplicate in and watch whether the warning catches it. That is the whole test.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: I want to push on the evidence. A proposed workflow and a vendor-documented capability are not a customer result.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Completely correct, and I will not dress it up. No measured time saving, no real implementation, no outcome to report. The logic Claude generates can be wrong. You inspect the output yourself before it gets anywhere near a real group or event.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So the unassigned plates are still your problem.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Entirely your problem. The artifact makes the gap visible. Closing it is on the humans doing the reviewing.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Jamie, you are extremely worked up about a checklist for a fictional picnic.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Rufus, you once described a spreadsheet as "pretty much fine" and then three people ordered the same catering item for a team lunch.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That was a supply chain issue.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: It really wasn't.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: One real limitation before anyone opens Claude. Artifacts need code execution enabled in your account. That is not a default everywhere. Check your settings first, because assuming it is available and finding it isn't is its own coordination failure.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So what does someone do right now?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Open Claude. Invent five names. Assign fictional items. Ask for a small assignment checklist as an artifact. Manually add a duplicate and read the output line by line before you trust any of it. Keep everything synthetic. The coordination still belongs to the people.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Low stakes, concrete, honest about what it cannot do.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That is the standard. The artifact just surfaces the gaps before someone arrives holding the third bag of crisps nobody requested.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I'll try it. And I'll confirm who has the plates this time.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Write that down. And maybe the forks.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's Jamie's AI transformation.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Alright. We asked at the top whether Google's on-premises AI chips can actually solve your agentic bottlenecks. Here's what we know.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: If you're blocked by data-residency rules — if your legal or compliance team won't let your sensitive data leave your building — then Google's new on-prem TPU option is a legitimate thing to evaluate. That problem is real, and this addresses it.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: If you're not blocked by those requirements, the case is much less clear. We don't have independent performance benchmarks, we don't have public pricing, and nearly a hundred customers is a beginning, not a proof of scale.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So the honest answer is: it's a real option for a specific set of organizations, and an interesting early signal for everyone else. Watch the benchmark numbers, and watch whether that customer count grows.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The question we'd leave you with this week — and this is genuinely something to think about, not just a clever closing. When you hear about an AI hardware option that promises to put the chip in your building, does that actually mean control? Or does it just mean the leash is longer?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That is a question worth sitting with.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Send us your answer. You know where to find us. Leave a comment, leave a review, those genuinely help more people find the show.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: We're on every platform you use. Find us, follow us, and bring a question.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Starting with this one. Today’s question for you: When your workplace tools add 'proactive' AI features, do you find them helpful or just another layer of distraction?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: A quick final note: today’s episode was brought to you by The Ledger—decision-grade AI signal for people who cannot afford to be late.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What changed. Who wins. What you do next. That’s The AI Edge. Follow The AI Edge now. Join us tomorrow for what changes next.
